results.1:
Two arms: exit 0; prints
top_p: 1e+20
...
  b: 1e-07
One arm: exit 0; prints with an added .0:
top_p: 1.0e+20
...
  b: 1.0e-07
(In all three, `.inf`, `.nan`, `2.0` and `-0.0` are shown as is. Only the arm that accepted `-.inf` lists `- -.inf` under weights.)
results.2:
All three arms: exit 0; prints
top_p: 1e+20
...
  b: 1e-07
(`.inf`, `.nan`, `2.0` and `-0.0` are shown as is)

context.in_practice: Both routes write infinity and NaN as `.inf`/`.nan` and keep `2.0` and `-0.0`. Where they differ is exponent numbers. Most arms write `1e+20`/`1e-07`, or keep what you typed (`1e20`). Strict YAML 1.1 readers do not treat an exponent number without a decimal point as a number, so they read those back as text. Only one route 1 arm shows `1.0e+20`/`1.0e-07`, which every reader loads as a number, and that arm still writes `1e+20` to the file itself. Whether `-.inf` can be set at all depends on the command-line parsing, not on this choice: one route 1 arm accepted it, and the other five arms rejected it as a missing value.
context.stakes: This decides how decimal numbers, infinity and NaN are written to the YAML config and shown back. If they are written badly, some YAML readers load a value as text instead of a number, or a value like `-.inf` cannot be set at all.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 handles special values on purpose, but its arms produce three different outputs. Route 2 gives nearly the same results by default, with no deliberate handling of numbers that some readers load back as text.

plan_why: Writes non-finite and exponent floats into the file (changed value, new key, list item, new mapping) and prints a section as YAML, showing whether floats come out as repr text, as .inf/-.inf/.nan, or with an added .0 (e.g. 1e+20 vs 1.0e+20), and whether they read back as floats.
